question.worked_solution:
We break up the integral as follows:

$$
{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x
$$

First, we calculate the antiderivative using a substitution. Let $u=1+{x}^{2}$,  then $\text{d}u=2x\text{d}x.$ Hence,

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{u}+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

We now evaluate the first of the improper integrals, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }{\int }_{a}^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={lim}_{a\to -\infty }({-\frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}|}_{a}^{0}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(\frac{1}{1+0}-\frac{1}{1+{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-{lim}_{a\to -\infty }(1-\frac{1}{1+{a}^{2}}) \\  & =-1+0 \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, notice that the integrand is an **odd** function. This means that we can immediately deduce that 

$$
{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x=1.
$$

Therefore, since both improper integrals exist, we conclude that 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-\infty }^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & ={\int }_{-\infty }^{0}\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x+{\int }_{0}^{\infty }\frac{2x}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-1+1 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
